extracted.intended_audience: researchers, grant administrators, policymakers, and peer reviewers interested in grant funding evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Assessment of how well NIH peer review percentile scores predict subsequent grant productivity (publications and citations) for funded grants. Focuses on analysis methods and outcome metrics used to judge predictive performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentile score (NIH peer review panel ranking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentile scores awarded by peer review panels to rank grant applications; the lowest percentile scores are the most favorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by NIH to prioritize funding (highest-ranked applications receive funding). The paper reports these percentile scores are a poor discriminator of subsequent productivity: random-forest analysis shows percentile explains ~0.98% of variance in productivity and ROC AUC for predicting above-median citation productivity is 0.54 (95% CI 0.53–0.54). Notes that rounding to whole numbers and changes in the NIH percentiling algorithm (since 2009) affect the distribution (fewer zeros). Typical success rates (context) can be as low as ~10%, which amplifies limitations of relying on percentiles alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication productivity (number of publications acknowledging grant within five years)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of publications that acknowledge support from a grant within five years of grant approval (data from PubMed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as one primary outcome measure of grant productivity. In the analysed cohort, grants in the top half by publication productivity had ≥6 publications. Figures present mean publications per percentile score with SDM error bars; statistical comparisons performed (one-way ANOVA) to identify significant differences across percentile cohorts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation productivity (total citations of grant-supported papers up to a cutoff date)
rubrics_metrics.description: Total number of citations received by the papers acknowledging a grant, measured until the end of 2013 (data from Web of Science).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as another primary outcome measure of grant productivity. In the analysed cohort, grants in the top half by citation productivity had ≥128 citations. Citation productivity was used to construct ROC curves (high vs low productivity relative to median) to evaluate how well percentile predicts impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohort selection by percentile cutoff (analysis limited to percentile ≤20)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis restricted to funded grants that had percentile scores of 20 or better (most favorable 20 percentiles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study re-analysed 102,740 funded grants with percentile scores ≤20. This cohort selection frames the conclusions about the discriminative ability of percentile scores within the range typically considered for funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) and area under the curve (AUC) to assess predictive performance
rubrics_metrics.description: ROC/AUC used to evaluate how well percentile score predicts binary productivity outcomes (e.g., citation productivity greater than the median).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported AUC = 0.54 (95% CI 0.53–0.54), where AUC=1.0 is a perfect predictor and AUC=0.5 indicates chance-level performance. An AUC of 0.54 implies only marginal predictive ability above chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-learning (random forest) model: variance explained
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-parametric random forest model (500 trees) constructed to evaluate grant percentile score as a predictor of citation productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results indicate percentile score accounts for 0.98% of variance in productivity (very small explanatory power). The mean of squared residuals converged to 366,620 in the model, underscoring weak predictive contribution of percentile alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical comparison and significance testing across percentile cohorts
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison of mean publication and citation counts across different percentile scores using statistical tests (e.g., one-way ANOVA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures show mean productivity per percentile with SDM error bars; pink bars indicate cohorts significantly different from all cohorts with poorer scores by one-way ANOVA. Many adjacent percentile cohorts do not differ significantly, indicating weak discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive standard: limitations of peer review as a predictor of downstream productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptual criterion that peer review rankings (percentiles) are intended to predict which applications will produce the most productive research outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues that percentile-based peer review has limited ability to predict productivity, particularly given low funding success rates; this suggests caution in over-relying on percentile rank as a quality signal for funding allocation.
